title: Fentanyl: Actually As Dangerous As They Say
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with iHeart intro voice) give an overview of fentanyl: its origin as a surgical anesthetic developed by Paul Janssen in Belgium, how illicit fentanyl became the deadliest street drug in the US, the three waves of the opioid crisis, why overdose deaths rose despite falling use, the iron law of prohibition, smoking and pill-form fentanyl, overdose mechanics and breathing suppression, harm reduction (test strips, Narcan, safe use sites), medication-assisted treatment, myths about immigrants, homelessness and touching fentanyl, recent declines in deaths and cross-border interdiction. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about Black characters dying first in disaster and horror movies.

entities.name: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

segments.title: Opening and introduction
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on fentanyl and note a possible decline in deaths.

segments.title: Fentanyl origins and potency
segments.summary: Fentanyl is a synthetic opioid, far more potent than morphine and heroin, developed by Paul Janssen in Belgium as a surgical anesthetic from the my paradine base. Changes to fat solubility speed onset and shorten duration. It reached Europe in 1963 and the US in 1968, approved with droperidol, with restrictions later loosened. Effects and risks are described, and it is a Schedule II drug.

segments.title: Illicit fentanyl and analogs
segments.summary: Illicit fentanyl differs from the pharmaceutical version. Carfentanil and sufentanil are named as analogs; carfentanil is used to sedate large animals and is far stronger than fentanyl.

segments.title: Street names and drug combinations
segments.summary: Street names such as Tango and Cash are mentioned, referring to fentanyl mixed with cocaine or methamphetamine, which produces speedball-type combinations.

segments.title: Three waves of the opioid crisis
segments.summary: The opioid crisis is described in three waves: prescription opioids in the 1990s, heroin after OxyContin reformulation around 2010, and the fentanyl wave from about 2013. Death rates per 100,000 rose from 2 in 1999 to 8 in 2013 to 25 in 2022. Fentanyl deaths in 2022 were about 76,226, and life expectancy effects are discussed for middle-aged white adults without college degrees. The Dope Sick series is referenced.

segments.title: Drivers of deaths and disease of despair
segments.summary: Overdose deaths are linked to economic hardship and low social capital rather than simply more users. Fentanyl's increased danger, not rising use, is said to explain the rise in deaths.

segments.title: Iron law of prohibition and fentanyl's spread
segments.summary: The iron law of prohibition, coined by economist Richard Cowan in 1986, is discussed as a reason for fentanyl's rise. Fentanyl's potency makes it cheap to smuggle. A 2020 Addiction study suggests dealers drove its introduction to cut costs. Fentanyl share in heroin rose from under 1 percent to 40 percent between 2013 and 2021, and users often did not know the potency.

segments.title: Route of use and pills
segments.summary: Fentanyl produces a fast head rush and short high, raising overdose risk. Smoking rose sharply among fatal overdoses while injection fell. Fentanyl pills made to look like M30 OxyContin pills and fentanyl found in cocaine and other drugs cause accidental overdoses.

segments.title: Fentanyl production, smuggling and myths
segments.summary: Precursors come mainly from China, which banned fentanyl production in 2019 but manufacturers continued. Cartels in Mexico produce and distribute it. Myths are addressed: most fentanyl enters through legal points of entry, smuggled by US citizens (Cato Institute: 86.3 percent of convicted smugglers are American citizens), not illegal immigrants. The Sinaloa cartel bans selling fentanyl under penalty of death.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Ad break before the harm reduction discussion.

segments.title: Drug policy, harm reduction, and Narcan
segments.summary: Fentanyl is treated more as a public health crisis than in past crack-era policy, partly because it was seen as a white issue. Harm reduction tools include drug test strips, which detect fentanyl but not dose or analog, supervised use sites, staggered dosing, and naloxone (Narcan), with a personal anecdote about its use.

segments.title: Overdose mechanics and first response
segments.summary: Opioids suppress breathing through receptors in the brainstem (medulla and pons), voluntary breathing centers, and the CO2-sensing system. Overdoses may also cause aspiration from suppressed gag reflex. Signs include froth from the mouth; sternal rubbing and calling 911 and administering naloxone are recommended.

segments.title: Medication-assisted treatment and tolerance
segments.summary: Medication-assisted treatment with methadone or buprenorphine is the gold standard for opioid use disorder, with access barriers and stigma. A CDC study from 2022 reported only about 25 percent of those needing MAT receive it. Prison withdrawal and loss of tolerance raise overdose risk after release.

segments.title: Myths about touching fentanyl and homelessness
segments.summary: Myths that brief skin contact or inhalation of fentanyl causes overdose are discussed, with a 2016 DEA advisory mentioned and nocebo effects described. Homelessness is attributed mainly to housing costs rather than drugs.

segments.title: Declining deaths and interdiction
segments.summary: Opioid deaths peaked in 2022 at about 108,000 and are expected to fall 15 to 20 percent in 2024. Reasons include harm reduction, fewer active users, and younger generations using fewer drugs. Cooperation with Mexico reduced fentanyl seizures at the border by about 20 percent in 2024. Closing advice recommends seeking help and not starting.

segments.title: Listener mail on Black characters in disaster movies
segments.summary: Listeners Kevin and Serena respond to a question about Black characters dying first in horror and disaster films. The hosts also mention Richard Roundtree surviving in Earthquake.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener email and close the episode.
